program_primer_markdown:
# Start here — data engineering background, new to AI

You already know **pipelines, tables, and tests**. This program teaches **AI in the same order**: plain words first, then short videos, then small code you can run.

## What is an LLM?

An **LLM** (Large Language Model) is software that **reads text and writes text**. It is not your warehouse and it does not run SQL for you. Think of it as a very fast assistant that can summarize, classify, or draft structured answers—**but it can be wrong**, so you check outputs like you check for bad rows after a load.

## How this studio is laid out

| Panel | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| **Left** | Courses **0 → 15** in order. Click the next course when the Prove gate is done. |
| **Middle** | Topics for that course—work **top to bottom**. The first topic says **START HERE**. |
| **Center** | **Theory (Foundations)** → **Lecture** → **Lab & Prove** for the topic you selected. |
| **Right** | Notes and optional mentor (Settings → API key). |

## Rules that keep you from getting lost

1. **One topic at a time** — finish the checkbox objective, not the whole YouTube channel.
2. **Theory before lecture** — open **Foundations** theory until the words make sense, then watch.
3. **Optional means skip for now** — come back when you have time.
4. **Prove ends the month** — paste a GitHub (or other) link when the rubric is met.

## What you build over ~15 months

One practice project on GitHub (synthetic or public data only) that grows each course:

| When | You add |
| --- | --- |
| Course 0 | Typed JSON from messy text + golden-set score |
| Course 1 | Gateway logs: model, tokens, latency, cost |
| Courses 2–3 | Workflow + safe tools |
| Courses 4–6 | Search and document chunks |
| Courses 7–9 | Tests in CI + policy + traces |
| Courses 10–12 | Full demo + deploy + lineage sample |
| Courses 13–15 | Portfolio and interviews |

## Your first 30 minutes

1. On the **home** page, click **Start step 1 — What is an LLM?**
2. Read **Theory** on **Foundations**.
3. Watch the **Lecture** (about one hour).
4. Write three notes: what is a **token**, what is a **context limit**, one way the model can be **wrong**.

## Theory levels

| Level | When to use it |
| --- | --- |
| **Foundations** | **Default** — start here on every new topic. |
| Study guide | After Foundations feels easy on that topic. |
| Platform depth | Tradeoffs, metrics, failures—when you want staff-level depth. |

Mark a topic complete when **this line’s** goal is met—not when you finish every video on the internet.

glossary.de_analogy: Like a max batch size—overflow means truncate, summarize, or chunk.

glossary.definition: Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
glossary.de_analogy: Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.

glossary.definition: Model output that looks plausible but is factually wrong or unsupported.
glossary.de_analogy: Bad join or null handling that still returns a row—never trust without validation.

glossary.definition: Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
glossary.de_analogy: Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.

glossary.definition: Python library for data validation and settings using type hints.
glossary.de_analogy: Runtime schema checks like Great Expectations on a single record.

glossary.de_analogy: Retry loop around a flaky API until the payload passes JSON schema.

glossary.definition: Gateway that routes requests to many model providers with one API.
glossary.de_analogy: API gateway + provider failover for model endpoints.

glossary.definition: Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks.
glossary.de_analogy: Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.

glossary.definition: Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.
glossary.de_analogy: Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.

glossary.definition: Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change.
glossary.de_analogy: pytest + data diff job in CI.

glossary.definition: Business rule beyond JSON shape (e.g. balances sum to zero).
glossary.de_analogy: Custom SQL tests or domain constraints.

glossary.definition: Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output.
glossary.de_analogy: Time-to-first-byte on an API response.

glossary.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model.
glossary.de_analogy: Join to a reference table before computing a metric.

glossary.definition: Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
glossary.de_analogy: Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.

glossary.definition: Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
glossary.de_analogy: Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.

glossary.definition: Persisted graph state so a run can resume after failure or interrupt.
glossary.de_analogy: Idempotent checkpoint in Spark/Flink or workflow saga state.

glossary.definition: Human-in-the-loop: pause automation for review before continuing.
glossary.de_analogy: Manual approval step in a pipeline.

glossary.definition: System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
glossary.de_analogy: Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.

glossary.definition: Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models.
glossary.de_analogy: Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.

glossary.definition: JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts.
glossary.de_analogy: API request body contract.

glossary.definition: Append-only record of who invoked which tool with what outcome.
glossary.de_analogy: CloudTrail / data access logs for compliance.

glossary.definition: Metric got worse vs baseline on the golden set after a change.
glossary.de_analogy: CI test failure on main metrics.

glossary.definition: Secondary model or provider used when the primary fails or is slow.
glossary.de_analogy: Secondary region or read replica failover.

glossary.definition: How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p).
glossary.de_analogy: Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.

glossary.definition: Mechanism for the model to weigh which input tokens matter for each output token.
glossary.de_analogy: Weighted join keys—without math depth, just “focus mechanism.”

# Karpathy — Intro to LLMs

> **Foundations** — plain language first. When this makes sense, open **Lecture**. Switch to **Study guide** for the full checklist and prove rubric.

## What is this, in plain English?

Karpathy explains LLMs as next-token predictors: training vs inference, why they sound confident when wrong, and what a context window really means.

**Why it shows up now:** Every later topic assumes you know the model is not a database—you validate outputs like bad rows in a pipeline.

## Mental model

LLM = stateless text function with a max input size; your platform owns schemas, retries, and tests around it.

When Karpathy talks about tokens, think **columns in a wide string**: the model only sees a limited window at once. When he talks about hallucination, think **synthetic rows** that pass a vibe check but fail a join to ground truth.

## Words you will hear

- **Token** — A chunk of text the model reads or generates; billing and context limits are counted in tokens.
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* Like rows or bytes processed—your cost and SLA driver.
- **Context window** — Maximum tokens the model can consider in one request (prompt + completion).
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* Like a max batch size—overflow means truncate, summarize, or chunk.
- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.

## While you watch

- Training vs inference—what runs in your AWS bill monthly
- Context window as a hard limit (truncation policy)
- Why scale changes capability but not the need for verification
- Sampling / temperature as a stability lever for extraction

## This month you are working toward

- Structured extraction with Instructor, Pydantic, LiteLLM, pytest
- Retry loops and invariant validators on messy logs

## Ready for the lecture when

You can sketch input → model → validated JSON on one diagram.

# Karpathy — Intro to LLMs

> **Visual study guide** · Course 0 boot sprint · ~1 h video · Primary: [YouTube ↗](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zjkBMFhNj_g)

## What you are learning

Large language models are **not databases**. They are **next-token predictors**: given a sequence of tokens, they output a probability distribution over the next token, repeatedly, until a stop condition. Your platform job is to wrap that unreliable function with **contracts, budgets, and tests**—the same way you would wrap any flaky external API.

| Concept | Plain English | Platform lever |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Token** | Chunk of text the model reads/writes | Billing, context limits, log truncation |
| **Context window** | Max tokens in one request | Chunking, summarization, rejection |
| **Training vs inference** | Learn weights vs run weights | You almost always ship **inference** only |
| **Hallucination** | Plausible but false text | Schema validation, golden sets, HITL |
| **Temperature** | Randomness of sampling | Lower for extraction; higher for brainstorming |

## System picture: where the LLM sits

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph YourPlatform["Your platform (you own this)"]
    IN[Ingest logs / events]
    GW[Gateway auth budget routing]
    VAL[Pydantic / invariants]
    STORE[(Warehouse / stage DB)]
    IN --> GW --> LLM
    LLM --> VAL --> STORE
  end
  subgraph Provider["Model provider"]
    LLM[LLM inference API]
  end
  OPS[Metrics alerts eval CI] -.-> GW
  OPS -.-> VAL
```

Karpathy’s talk explains what happens **inside** the `LLM` box. This track focuses on everything **around** it.

## Training vs inference (two different jobs)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Train["Training (offline, rare for you)"]
    D[(Huge corpus)] --> GPU[GPU cluster weeks]
    GPU --> W[Weight files]
  end
  subgraph Infer["Inference (online, daily)"]
    P[Prompt tokens] --> API[Hosted API]
    API --> O[Completion tokens]
  end
  W -.->|weights shipped to provider| API
```

- **Training** — expensive, infrequent, not your month-1 deliverable.
- **Inference** — per-request cost, latency SLOs, retries, and logging **every** call.

## Mental model: LLM as a stateless function

Treat each call as:

\[
\text{completion} = f(\text{prompt}, \text{model\_id}, \text{params})
\]

There is **no memory** between calls unless **you** persist chat history, RAG chunks, or graph state.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant GW as Gateway
  participant M as Model
  App->>GW: prompt + max_tokens + temperature
  GW->>M: routed request
  M-->>GW: token stream
  GW-->>App: completion + usage metadata
  Note over App: You log prompt_hash model version usage
```

## While you watch (checklist)

- [ ] Sketch **training vs inference** on one page.
- [ ] Note **context window** as a hard limit—what happens when logs exceed it?
- [ ] List three reasons the model sounds **confident when wrong**.
- [ ] Write **temperature** guidance for extraction vs creative tasks.
- [ ] Identify what you will **log** per request (model id, tokens, latency, prompt hash).

## Failure modes (design for these early)

| Failure | Symptom | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trusting prose | Bad data in warehouse | Pydantic + invariants + golden set |
| Huge prompts | Cost spike, timeout | Truncate, summarize, structured chunks |
| No audit trail | Cannot replay incident | Log prompt hash, model version, params |
| Unbounded retries | 10× cost on bad rows | Cap retries; fail to HITL queue |

## How this connects to boot-week prove

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  K[Karpathy mental model] --> P[Pydantic contracts]
  P --> I[Instructor retries]
  I --> G[LiteLLM gateway]
  G --> T[pytest golden set]
```

You are not proving you trained a model—you are proving you can **ship a bounded, testable extraction path**.

## Done when

You can draw **input → gateway → model → validated JSON → storage** and explain what you **never** trust without a schema check.

## Primary source

[Karpathy — Intro to LLMs ↗](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zjkBMFhNj_g) — mark this topic complete when **this video’s objectives** are met, not when you finish unrelated playlists.

# Karpathy — Intro to LLMs

> **Platform depth** — engineering judgment: tradeoffs, metrics, failures, interviews. Read **Study guide** first if you have not done the checklist.

## Platform narrative (this topic)

Platform framing: treat inference as a **multi-tenant, rate-limited dependency** with fat-tailed latency. Capacity planning starts with tokens-per-record distributions on your golden set, not GPU specs. Security: prompt injection is input validation; never concatenate untrusted log lines into system prompts without sanitization boundaries. For interviews, articulate pretrain/finetune/prompt/RAG as a **cost ladder**—you default to prompt+schema until evals prove you need the next rung.

## Rollout and implementation depth

Use this video to draw a one-page diagram: **training** (offline, expensive, not your job in this track) vs **inference** (online API calls you pay per token). Note three production knobs you will reuse in Course 1: max tokens, temperature, and timeout. After watching, write a README section ‘What we trust the model for’ vs ‘What we always validate’—that becomes your team policy seed.

## Architecture anchor

LLM = stateless text function with a max input size; your platform owns schemas, retries, and tests around it.

## Primary source focus

- Training vs inference—what runs in your AWS bill monthly
- Context window as a hard limit (truncation policy)
- Why scale changes capability but not the need for verification
- Sampling / temperature as a stability lever for extraction

## Failure modes to design for

- Treating model prose as ground truth without schema validation
- Unbounded prompts on large logs → cost spikes and timeouts
- No logging of prompt hash + model version for incident replay

## Metrics and alerts

- Task success rate on golden set (tier 1)

- Schema validation pass rate (tier 0)

- Cost per 1k successful extractions

## Tradeoffs (explicit)

- **Depth vs shipping:** more videos rarely beat one golden-set iteration.
- **Generalist model vs fine-tune:** default generalist + schema until evals prove otherwise.

## Decision record (fill before you ship)

| Stance | Your choice | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adopt now | … | Why Karpathy — Intro to LLMs is in scope this month |
| Experiment | … | What you will measure in two weeks |
| Defer | … | What risk you accept by waiting |

## Interview depth

- Explain LLMs to a data engineer without saying ‘AI magic.’
- Where would you enforce max context for log extraction?
- How do you detect and respond to a provider outage?

## Capstone implementation

README: 3 bullets—failure mode, log field, test you will add.

## Advanced done bar

You can sketch input → model → validated JSON on one diagram.

# DeepLearning.AI — Pydantic for LLM Workflows

> **Platform depth** — engineering judgment: tradeoffs, metrics, failures, interviews. Read **Study guide** first if you have not done the checklist.

## Platform narrative (this topic)

Schema evolution: version models (`LogEventV1`) and migrate with shadow validation before flipping prod. Custom validators belong at the boundary; do not sprinkle business rules inside prompt text only. Measure **validation error taxonomy** (missing field vs wrong enum vs semantic wrong amount) separately in metrics—retries help syntax, not semantics. Interview: compare Pydantic validation to Great Expectations / JSON Schema in a CDC stream.

# Instructor — quick start

> **Visual study guide** · Course 0 · Read · Primary: [python.useinstructor.com ↗](https://python.useinstructor.com/)

## What Instructor adds

**Pydantic** defines the shape. **Instructor** forces the LLM to fill that shape—or retry until validation passes (within your limits).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  RAW[Raw log line or document]
  PROMPT[Prompt + response_model=LogEvent]
  LLM[Chat completion API]
  PARSE[Parse JSON into Pydantic]
  OK{Valid?}
  RETRY[Repair / retry with error context]
  OUT[Typed LogEvent record]

  RAW --> PROMPT --> LLM --> PARSE --> OK
  OK -->|yes| OUT
  OK -->|no| RETRY --> LLM
```

Without Instructor you manually: call API → parse JSON → `model_validate` → catch errors → rewrite prompt. Instructor standardizes that loop.

## Architecture in your capstone repo

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Boundary["Trust boundary"]
    EXT[External logs]
  end
  subgraph App["reconciler / extractor"]
    INS[instructor.patch client]
    MOD[LogEvent schema]
    INV[Business invariants]
  end
  subgraph Provider["LiteLLM / provider"]
    API[chat.completions]
  end
  EXT --> INS
  INS --> API
  API --> INS
  INS --> MOD --> INV
```

## Core objects

| Piece | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `BaseModel` | Field types, required vs optional, enums |
| `instructor.patch(...)` | Wrap client; add `response_model` to calls |
| `ValidationError` | Signal to retry or route to HITL |
| Custom validators | Rules JSON shape alone cannot express |

## Retry policy (decide explicitly)

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Call
  Call --> Valid: schema OK
  Call --> Retry: ValidationError
  Retry --> Call: attempts < max
  Retry --> DeadLetter: attempts >= max
  Valid --> [*]
  DeadLetter --> [*]
```

| Policy | When to use |
| --- | --- |
| 2–3 retries with error text | Noisy logs, cheap model |
| 0 retries, fail fast | High-stakes finance rows |
| Repair prompt | Missing optional fields only |

## Read path for this topic

1. Quick start — minimal `response_model` example.
2. Retries — how validation errors feed the next attempt.
3. Partial / streaming — **defer** until Month 1 build unless syllabus asks.

## Failure modes

- **Silent coercion** — using loose parsing; always prefer strict models.
- **Giant schemas** — every field in the tool schema burns tokens; start minimal.
- **Retries without metrics** — you cannot tune cost if retry rate is invisible.

## Metrics to log

- `schema_validation_pass_rate`
- `retry_count_per_record`
- `usd_per_successful_extraction`
- `validation_error_code` (taxonomy: missing field, wrong enum, invariant)

## Done when

You can implement `extract(text) -> LogEvent` with Instructor + explicit `ValidationError` handling and one pytest on a golden row.

## Primary source

[Instructor documentation ↗](https://python.useinstructor.com/) — shared across multiple syllabus topics; finish **quick start + retries** for this checkbox only.

lessons.content:
## 🏗️ Architectural Overview
A typical GPT model uses a decoder-only transformer architecture. 

### Core Components:
1. **Token Embeddings:** Maps vocabulary to dense vectors.
2. **Positional Encoding:** Injects sequence order.
3. **Self-Attention Blocks:** Captures relationships.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

class Head(nn.Module):
    \"\"\" one head of self-attention \"\"\"
    def __init__(self, head_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.key = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.query = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.value = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.register_buffer("tril", torch.tril(torch.ones(block_size, block_size)))

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        k = self.key(x)   
        q = self.query(x) 
        wei = q @ k.transpose(-2,-1) * C**-0.5 
        wei = wei.masked_fill(self.tril[:T, :T] == 0, float("-inf"))
        wei = F.softmax(wei, dim=-1)
        v = self.value(x) 
        return wei @ v 
```

### 🧠 Mathematical Intuition
$$ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V $$

### 🛡️ Production Invariants
- Always enforce `B, T, C` tensor shape contracts.
- Apply `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_` to prevent gradient explosion.

## 🏗️ Architectural Overview
A typical GPT model uses a decoder-only transformer architecture. 

### Core Components:
1. **Token Embeddings:** Maps vocabulary to dense vectors.
2. **Positional Encoding:** Injects sequence order.
3. **Self-Attention Blocks:** Captures relationships.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

class Head(nn.Module):
    \"\"\" one head of self-attention \"\"\"
    def __init__(self, head_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.key = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.query = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.value = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.register_buffer("tril", torch.tril(torch.ones(block_size, block_size)))

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        k = self.key(x)   
        q = self.query(x) 
        wei = q @ k.transpose(-2,-1) * C**-0.5 
        wei = wei.masked_fill(self.tril[:T, :T] == 0, float("-inf"))
        wei = F.softmax(wei, dim=-1)
        v = self.value(x) 
        return wei @ v 
```

### 🧠 Mathematical Intuition
$$ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V $$

### 🛡️ Production Invariants
- Always enforce `B, T, C` tensor shape contracts.
- Apply `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_` to prevent gradient explosion.

# AI Agents in LangGraph

> **Visual study guide** · Course 2 · Video · [DL.AI short course ↗](https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/ai-agents-in-langgraph/)

## From one-shot extraction to a state machine

Month 1 treated the LLM as a **single function call**. Month 2 introduces **graphs**: nodes (steps), edges (transitions), and **persistent state** so runs can pause, resume, and survive failures.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Extract
  Extract --> Validate: JSON OK
  Extract --> Repair: validation fail
  Repair --> Extract
  Validate --> Stage: invariants pass
  Validate --> HITL: invariants fail
  HITL --> Validate: human fix
  Stage --> [*]
```

## LangGraph vocabulary

| Term | Meaning | Data-engineering analogy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **State** | Typed dict carried through the graph | Pipeline run context |
| **Node** | Function that updates state | Task / operator |
| **Edge** | Allowed transition | DAG dependency |
| **Checkpoint** | Persisted state snapshot | Idempotent checkpoint / saga |
| **Interrupt** | Pause for human input | Approval step in Airflow |

## reconciler-agent architecture (your prove target)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph Graph["LangGraph"]
    N1[ingest_node]
    N2[extract_node]
    N3[validate_node]
    N4[stage_node]
    N1 --> N2 --> N3 --> N4
  end
  CP[(SQLite or Postgres checkpointer)]
  Graph <-->|read/write state| CP
  MCP[MCP tools] -.-> N2
  GW[LiteLLM] -.-> N2
```

## Checkpointing: why it matters

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Worker
  participant Graph
  participant CP as Checkpointer
  Worker->>Graph: invoke(thread_id)
  Graph->>CP: save state after node
  Note over Worker: process crash
  Worker->>Graph: resume(thread_id)
  Graph->>CP: load last snapshot
  Graph-->>Worker: continue from safe node
```

- **SQLite** — local dev, single worker.
- **Postgres** — shared state for multiple workers (your production path).

## While you watch the course

- [ ] Map each DL.AI module to a **node** in your graph diagram.
- [ ] Note where **tools** are bound vs where **state** is updated.
- [ ] Identify the **interrupt** pattern for HITL (Month 10 capstone preview).
- [ ] List what you will persist in checkpoint tables (thread id, step, payload hash).

## MCP + LangGraph (preview of Course 3)

Tools should not be ad-hoc HTTP calls inside nodes—prefer **MCP** with audit logs (next month). For now, stub tools with clear interfaces.

## Failure modes

| Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| God-node graph | One node does everything—split by responsibility |
| No checkpoint | Cannot resume long runs |
| Unbounded loops | Max steps / cycle detection |
| Side effects before validate | Stage only after invariants pass |

## Done when

You can whiteboard **states, nodes, checkpoints, and one interrupt path** for `reconciler-agent` and explain why SQLite is not enough for multi-worker prod.

## Primary source

[AI Agents in LangGraph ↗](https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/ai-agents-in-langgraph/) — complete modules that match **this** syllabus line, not the entire LangChain catalog.

digest.title: LangGraph: Cyclic Agent State Machines
takeaways: Unlike linear DAGs (LangChain classic), LangGraph models agent loops as cyclic state graphs with explicit memory nodes and routing edges.
Every node is a function that receives State and returns partial state updates; reducers merge the state.
Supports durable execution with SQLite/Postgres checkpointers, allowing agents to pause, crash, and resume safely.
rules: Use interrupt() for Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) approval before executing high-risk tools (e.g. database writes).
Keep node functions pure and deterministic; push side-effects to tool nodes.
Always specify thread_id for conversation state isolation.
pitfalls: Creating infinite agent loops without a maximum iteration guard or step counter.
Passing large payloads inside state instead of storing artifacts in S3 and passing pointers.

# MCP introduction

> **Visual study guide** · Course 3 · Read · [modelcontextprotocol.io ↗](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction)

## Problem MCP solves

Agents need **tools** (query warehouse, run job, read ticket). Without a standard, every host invents its own plugin format. **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** defines how a **host** discovers and calls **tools** on a **server**—with schemas, auth boundaries, and audit-friendly requests.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Host["MCP host (Cursor, Claude Desktop, your agent)"]
    H[Orchestrator]
  end
  subgraph Server["MCP server (your service)"]
    T1[tool: run_query]
    T2[tool: fetch_schema]
    R[resources / prompts]
  end
  H <-->|JSON-RPC transport| Server
```

## Roles (memorize these)

| Role | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| **Host** | User session, model, when to call tools |
| **Client** | Connection from host to server (often embedded in host) |
| **Server** | Exposes tools/resources; enforces authz |

You will **build servers** and **consume** them from LangGraph nodes—not reimplement MCP inside every tool.

## Request lifecycle

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Host
  participant Server
  Host->>Server: initialize / list_tools
  Server-->>Host: tool schemas JSON Schema
  Host->>Server: call_tool(name, args)
  Server-->>Host: structured result or error
  Note over Server: Log caller tool args hash outcome
```

## Security architecture for Month 3 prove

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  AG[Agent / LangGraph node]
  MCP[MCP server]
  AUD[(Audit log)]
  SEC[Secrets via SM / env]
  DATA[(Warehouse read-only role)]
  AG --> MCP
  MCP --> AUD
  MCP --> SEC
  MCP --> DATA
```

Prove gate deliverables:

- README describing **tools**, **auth**, and **redacted** client config.
- No secrets in git—sample env only.

## How MCP relates to FastMCP (next reads)

| Layer | You learn |
| --- | --- |
| Spec (this topic) | Wire format, capabilities, transports |
| FastMCP | Python ergonomics to implement servers quickly |
| Your graph | Calls MCP instead of raw SQL in prompt text |

## Read checklist (official intro)

- [ ] Client vs server responsibilities
- [ ] Tool schema discovery (`list_tools`)
- [ ] Transports overview (stdio vs HTTP)—pick one for prove
- [ ] Resources vs tools vs prompts (don’t conflate)

## Failure modes

- **Tools without authz** — equivalent to public SQL endpoint.
- **Secrets in repo** — use redacted snippets in prove README only.
- **Unlogged tool calls** — compliance nightmare; append-only audit from day one.
- **Giant tool outputs** — truncate / paginate before model context.

## Done when

You can diagram **host → MCP server → backing system** and list three fields you log per `call_tool`.

## Primary source

[MCP introduction ↗](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction) then [specification ↗](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs) for depth as needed.

# FastMCP (Python)

> **Foundations** — plain language first. When this makes sense, open **Reading**. Switch to **Study guide** for the full checklist and prove rubric.

## What is this, in plain English?

FastMCP—Pythonic MCP server framework to ship tools quickly with type hints.

**Why it shows up now:** Implementation path for Month 3 build milestone.

## Mental model

FastMCP = FastAPI ergonomics for MCP tools.

Start from template; one tool end-to-end before adding many.

## Words you will hear

- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts.
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* API request body contract.
- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models.
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p).
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.

## While you read

- Quickstart
- Tools
- Testing

## This month you are working toward

- MCP client/server roles and tool schema discovery
- Read-only tools with JSONL audit log

## Ready after reading when

Local client can list tools.

### 1. In one sentence

FastMCP—Pythonic MCP server framework to ship tools quickly with type hints.

### 2. Why now in the track

Implementation path for Month 3 build milestone.

### 3. Core concepts

- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts. _DE angle:_ API request body contract.
- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models. _DE angle:_ Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p). _DE angle:_ Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt. _DE angle:_ Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **Eval harness** — Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change. _DE angle:_ pytest + data diff job in CI.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks. _DE angle:_ Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.

### 4. On the capstone repo

Scaffold FastMCP server with health check.

### 5. Done when

Local client can list tools.

# Tools: `lookup_schema`, `query_golden_set`, `run_readonly_sql` (sqlite)

> **Foundations** — plain language first. When this makes sense, open **Lecture**. Switch to **Study guide** for the full checklist and prove rubric.

## What is this, in plain English?

Build tools: lookup_schema, query_golden_set, run_readonly_query (allow-listed, safe).

**Why it shows up now:** First real MCP tools—read-only, auditable, least privilege.

## Mental model

Tools = parameterized stored procedures with guardrails.

Implement one tool completely before adding others.

## Words you will hear

- **Golden set** — Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.

# Document Chat RAG walkthrough

> **Foundations** — plain language first. When this makes sense, open **Lecture**. Switch to **Study guide** for the full checklist and prove rubric.

## What is this, in plain English?

Document Chat RAG walkthrough—end-to-end retrieval augmented generation on a doc corpus.

**Why it shows up now:** Month 4 introduces search-before-generate for your reconciler knowledge base.

## Mental model

RAG = join docs to question, then ask model with context.

Watch once; note chunking, embedding, retrieval, generation order.

## Words you will hear

- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
  - *Data pipeline analogy:* Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.

## While you watch

- Chunking
- Embedding model
- Retrieval k
- Answer grounding

- Dense + sparse (BM25) + **RRF** fusion
- recall@k on labeled questions

theory_levels.intermediate:
# Document Chat RAG walkthrough

> **Visual study guide** · Course 4 · Video · [YouTube walkthrough ↗](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zgnjMWipirk)

## What RAG is (one sentence)

**Retrieval-augmented generation**: fetch relevant chunks from a corpus, inject them into the prompt, then ask the model to answer **grounded in those chunks**—not from parametric memory alone.

Data-engineering analogy: **join to a reference table** before computing a metric.

## End-to-end RAG pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  DOC[Documents PDF MD logs]
  CHUNK[Chunking strategy]
  EMB[Embedding model]
  VDB[(Vector store e.g. pgvector)]
  Q[User query]
  RET[Top-k retrieval]
  PROMPT[Augmented prompt]
  LLM[LLM]
  ANS[Answer + citations]

  DOC --> CHUNK --> EMB --> VDB
  Q --> EMB --> RET
  VDB --> RET --> PROMPT --> LLM --> ANS
```

## Chunking is a data modeling choice

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Strategies["Common strategies"]
    FIX[Fixed token windows]
    SEC[Section / heading aware]
    REC[Recursive split]
  end
  FIX --> TRADE[Recall vs precision tradeoff]
  SEC --> TRADE
  REC --> TRADE
```

| Strategy | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed size | Simple | Splits tables / code badly |
| Heading-aware | Better docs | Needs structure metadata |
| Overlap windows | Higher recall | More storage & cost |

## Retrieval quality levers

- **Embedding model** — domain fit beats random OpenAI default for specialized logs.
- **k** — too few misses context; too many dilutes prompt.
- **Metadata filters** — tenant, date, source system (like partition pruning).
- **Hybrid** — BM25 + vectors for keyword-heavy queries (Month 4+ reads).

## Grounding and hallucination

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant User
  participant RAG
  participant Store
  User->>RAG: question
  RAG->>Store: similarity search
  Store-->>RAG: chunks + scores
  RAG->>RAG: build prompt with citations
  Note over RAG: If chunks empty refuse or escalate
  RAG-->>User: answer citing chunk ids
```

**Fail closed** when retrieval returns nothing relevant—do not let the model freestyle.

## While you watch

- [ ] Note **chunk size** and **overlap** used in the demo.
- [ ] Identify where **embeddings** are created vs queried.
- [ ] List what you would log: query, k, chunk ids, scores, model id.
- [ ] Sketch how pgvector fits your capstone (table DDL, index).

## Connect to pgvector prove (next reads)

```mermaid
erDiagram
  DOCUMENTS ||--o{ CHUNKS : contains
  CHUNKS {
    uuid id
    vector embedding
    text content
    jsonb metadata
  }
```

## Failure modes

| Issue | Signal | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stale index | Wrong doc version answers | Version source docs; re-embed on change |
| Chunk too large | Truncated context | Smaller chunks + parent retrieval |
| No citations | Untraceable answers | Require chunk ids in output schema |
| Injection via docs | Malicious corpus text | Sanitize sources; separate trust zones |

## Done when

You can draw **ingest → chunk → embed → store → retrieve → prompt → answer** and name one metric you will use in Month 7 eval (e.g. context precision).

## Primary source

[Document Chat RAG walkthrough ↗](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zgnjMWipirk) — then implement the pattern in your repo with **pgvector** per Course 4 build/prove items.

# Document Chat RAG walkthrough

> **Visual study guide** · Course 4 · Video · [YouTube walkthrough ↗](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zgnjMWipirk)

## What RAG is (one sentence)

**Retrieval-augmented generation**: fetch relevant chunks from a corpus, inject them into the prompt, then ask the model to answer **grounded in those chunks**—not from parametric memory alone.

Data-engineering analogy: **join to a reference table** before computing a metric.

## End-to-end RAG pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  DOC[Documents PDF MD logs]
  CHUNK[Chunking strategy]
  EMB[Embedding model]
  VDB[(Vector store e.g. pgvector)]
  Q[User query]
  RET[Top-k retrieval]
  PROMPT[Augmented prompt]
  LLM[LLM]
  ANS[Answer + citations]

  DOC --> CHUNK --> EMB --> VDB
  Q --> EMB --> RET
  VDB --> RET --> PROMPT --> LLM --> ANS
```

## Chunking is a data modeling choice

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Strategies["Common strategies"]
    FIX[Fixed token windows]
    SEC[Section / heading aware]
    REC[Recursive split]
  end
  FIX --> TRADE[Recall vs precision tradeoff]
  SEC --> TRADE
  REC --> TRADE
```

| Strategy | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed size | Simple | Splits tables / code badly |
| Heading-aware | Better docs | Needs structure metadata |
| Overlap windows | Higher recall | More storage & cost |

## Retrieval quality levers

- **Embedding model** — domain fit beats random OpenAI default for specialized logs.
- **k** — too few misses context; too many dilutes prompt.
- **Metadata filters** — tenant, date, source system (like partition pruning).
- **Hybrid** — BM25 + vectors for keyword-heavy queries (Month 4+ reads).

## Grounding and hallucination

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant User
  participant RAG
  participant Store
  User->>RAG: question
  RAG->>Store: similarity search
  Store-->>RAG: chunks + scores
  RAG->>RAG: build prompt with citations
  Note over RAG: If chunks empty refuse or escalate
  RAG-->>User: answer citing chunk ids
```

**Fail closed** when retrieval returns nothing relevant—do not let the model freestyle.

## While you watch

- [ ] Note **chunk size** and **overlap** used in the demo.
- [ ] Identify where **embeddings** are created vs queried.
- [ ] List what you would log: query, k, chunk ids, scores, model id.
- [ ] Sketch how pgvector fits your capstone (table DDL, index).

## Connect to pgvector prove (next reads)

```mermaid
erDiagram
  DOCUMENTS ||--o{ CHUNKS : contains
  CHUNKS {
    uuid id
    vector embedding
    text content
    jsonb metadata
  }
```

## Failure modes

| Issue | Signal | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stale index | Wrong doc version answers | Version source docs; re-embed on change |
| Chunk too large | Truncated context | Smaller chunks + parent retrieval |
| No citations | Untraceable answers | Require chunk ids in output schema |
| Injection via docs | Malicious corpus text | Sanitize sources; separate trust zones |

## Done when

You can draw **ingest → chunk → embed → store → retrieve → prompt → answer** and name one metric you will use in Month 7 eval (e.g. context precision).

## Primary source

[Document Chat RAG walkthrough ↗](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zgnjMWipirk) — then implement the pattern in your repo with **pgvector** per Course 4 build/prove items.

### 1. In one sentence

### 2. Why now in the track

### 3. Core concepts

- **RAG** — Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model. _DE angle:_ Join to a reference table before computing a metric.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search. _DE angle:_ Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts. _DE angle:_ API request body contract.
- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models. _DE angle:_ Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p). _DE angle:_ Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt. _DE angle:_ Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **Eval harness** — Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change. _DE angle:_ pytest + data diff job in CI.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks. _DE angle:_ Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.
- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text. _DE angle:_ Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.

### 4. On the capstone repo

Parser script with sample input/output in repo.

| **Primary source** | [Open link ↗](https://docling-project.github.io/docling/) |

## Study guide (five layers)

### 1. In one sentence

Docling (IBM)—document parsing pipeline for PDFs and office formats into structured content.

### 2. Why now in the track

Month 5 chunking starts with high-quality parse, not naive text strip.

### 3. Core concepts

- **RAG** — Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model. _DE angle:_ Join to a reference table before computing a metric.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search. _DE angle:_ Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts. _DE angle:_ API request body contract.
- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models. _DE angle:_ Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p). _DE angle:_ Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt. _DE angle:_ Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **Eval harness** — Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change. _DE angle:_ pytest + data diff job in CI.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks. _DE angle:_ Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.
- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text. _DE angle:_ Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.

### 4. On the capstone repo

Parser script with sample input/output in repo.

### 5. Done when

One doc parses reproducibly.

### Watch for

- Layout preservation
- Table handling
- Export formats

### Read these sections

- Table of contents → syllabus-named sections only

Choose parse path for your corpus formats; document limitations.

## Mental model

Docling = ETL from documents to structured blocks.

## Watch for failures

- Parser upgrades changing chunk hashes silently

## What this topic is about

Docling (IBM)—document parsing pipeline for PDFs and office formats into structured content.

Read for decisions, not coverage. For **Docling documentation**, end with: what API/pattern you would standardize, and what you would ban in code review.

**Why now:** Month 5 chunking starts with high-quality parse, not naive text strip.

## How this fits the course

These **course outcomes** are what you are building toward this month:

- PDF/HTML → chunks with page-level provenance
- Feed M4 index and capstone ingestion

## Step-by-step (time-boxed)

1. Open the primary doc for **Docling documentation**; scan headings and jump to sections tied to this course month.
2. Extract APIs, invariants, and anti-patterns — not trivia.
3. Decide adopt now / experiment / defer with one sentence of rationale.
4. Link any code spike or ADR in Lab & Prove if you built something.

- [Source repository](https://github.com/docling-project/docling) — Implementation reference after reading the docs.

## Study guide (five layers)

### 1. In one sentence

OpenTelemetry Python docs—vendor-neutral tracing if you outgrow single SaaS.

### 2. Why now in the track

Understand escape hatch from Langfuse-only instrumentation.

### 3. Core concepts

- **TTFT** — Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output. _DE angle:_ Time-to-first-byte on an API response.
- **Audit log** — Append-only record of who invoked which tool with what outcome. _DE angle:_ CloudTrail / data access logs for compliance.
- **Golden set** — Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes. _DE angle:_ Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.
- **RAG** — Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model. _DE angle:_ Join to a reference table before computing a metric.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search. _DE angle:_ Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts. _DE angle:_ API request body contract.
- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models. _DE angle:_ Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p). _DE angle:_ Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt. _DE angle:_ Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **Eval harness** — Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change. _DE angle:_ pytest + data diff job in CI.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks. _DE angle:_ Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.
- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text. _DE angle:_ Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.

Note OTel strategy in OBSERVABILITY.md.

- **TTFT** — Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output. _DE angle:_ Time-to-first-byte on an API response.

- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search. _DE angle:_ Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts. _DE angle:_ API request body contract.
- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models. _DE angle:_ Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p). _DE angle:_ Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.

- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text. _DE angle:_ Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.
